title: Bundles and Singles
big_idea: A number is tens and ones
child_idea: Ten single sticks make one bundle. A two-digit number tells us how many bundles and how many singles.

moe.note: Strand label for the tutor only. It is not a claim that the program covers the school syllabus, and it must not appear on child or parent pages as 'MOE-aligned'.

contest_moves: split a number into tens and ones
digit-clue puzzle (find the number from two clues)
objectives: Group up to 99 objects into bundles of ten and single ones, and say how many bundles and how many singles.
Read and write a two-digit number from a picture of bundles and singles, and the other way round.
Know that the left digit counts the tens and the right digit counts the ones, and that a 0 in the ones place means no singles.
Show that ten singles can be tied into one more bundle (5 tens 14 ones is 6 tens 4 ones).

remember: Ten and some more (11 to 19, then 20s and 30s)
joining_cold.assumes: Only counting to 20 and showing a number with fingers. Nothing from the holiday course is needed; if the child has done it, skip counting in 10s and bonds to 10 will feel familiar.
holiday_topics_revisited: Skip counting in 10s (Count with the Frog)
joining_cold.note: Lesson 1 is one of the hardest to miss in Term 1 (plan, section 2). A child who misses it watches the recording and does workbook pages 1 and 2 before Lesson 2.

child: About 50 small things of one kind: paper clips, dried pasta, buttons, lolly sticks or straws cut short
6 hair ties, rubber bands, small cups or pieces of string (to hold a bundle), or draw rings on paper
The printed workbook (pages 1 to 5) and the kit page (tens bars and ones squares), already cut out by a grown-up
A pencil, a rubber and spare paper
tutor: A slide deck and a tray of 30 lolly sticks or straws with three rubber bands to show on camera if you wish
A timer slide or a visible clock
kit_pages: Tens bars (9) and ones squares (20), printed on page 6 of the workbook; cut out before the lesson
materials.notes: No ruler is needed. Nothing needs to be bought: everything can be found at home. No matches, toothpicks or anything sharp. Small things never go near the mouth or ears.

timing.notes: Lesson 1 of the term has a 4-minute opening because it introduces the routine and the four inquirer rules. The last 5 minutes are the standing buffer; the optional Go further slide is used only if the lesson is on time.

sneak_peek.q1: Count the stars. Write how many. You may draw rings round groups to help.
sneak_peek.q2: Mei has 3 bundles of ten sticks and 4 single sticks. Ben has 34 sticks. Could they have the same number of sticks? Write yes or no, and why.
sneak_peek.a2: Yes. 3 bundles of ten is 30, and 4 more is 34.

opening.say: If you are watching the recording: hello! Get a pencil, paper, your workbook and your things to bundle. Pause or rewind any time.
opening.action: Gather your workbook, pencil, paper and things to bundle. Press play when ready.

remember.say: Recording: join in! Say the numbers out loud and show your fingers. Pause if you need longer.
remember.action: Play along. Say and show each answer before the video does.

sneak.say: Recording: pause now and try both puzzles on your paper. Guessing is fine. Press play for the next part.
sneak.action: Pause. Try both puzzles on your own paper. A guess is fine.

explore.say: Recording: pause now. Grab a handful, make bundles of ten, then build the numbers I call. Press play when you have tried.
explore.action: Pause. Grab and bundle, then build each number with your kit. Write what you find.

mini.say: Recording: keep watching and copy the examples. Rewind if you miss a step.
mini.action: Watch and copy the examples. Rewind any step you missed.

break.say: Recording: stand up and join in! Big jump for a ten, small hop for a one.
break.action: Stand up and jump the tens and hop the ones.

work.action: Pause. Do page 1, then play to check. Then page 2. Then choose a page to try.

exit.action: Pause. Do the exit ticket alone, then play to check it.

lines.text: @rec

Good morning, inquirers! Cameras on, pencil ready, your things to bundle on the table. This lesson is recorded so that a friend who is away can catch up. We record me and the screen only. You may switch your camera off whenever you like.
Here is our plan. A warm-up, two puzzles, then we explore with real things. Then I teach you a trick, we stretch, and you work in your workbook.
Four inquirer rules. Notice it: look closely. Test it: try it with real things. Explain why: say how you know. Mistakes help us: a guess is fine and you can always pass.
A shopkeeper has 47 pencils to count for a customer. Counting one by one is slow, and it is easy to lose count.
What could the shopkeeper do to count faster? Tell your screen or your grown-up.
Today we learn the shopkeeper's trick: bundles of ten.
Greet each child by first name and check their camera shows the page and hands.
Lesson 1 only: show the routine slide for 20 seconds and name the phases; do not read the table. Tell the group that recordings show only you and the screen.
@rec
Stand up if you can. We clap on every number. Count in tens with me: ten, twenty, thirty, all the way to one hundred.
Count in tens together, clapping, to 100. Then back from 100 to 0, whispering, shouting on 50.
Fingers to ten. I say a number. Show me how many more fingers make ten.
Six. How many more to make ten?
Three?
Eight?
Five?
Nine?
Ten and some more. Look at the full ten-frame and the extra counters.
Ten and three more makes?
Ten and six more?
Twenty and four more?
Thirty and seven more?

If a child hesitates on 24 or 37, say the tens word slowly (twenty... four) and point to the tens and the ones in the picture. Do not move on until most children have answered; this idea is the lesson.
Answers: 4, 7, 2, 5, 1 then 13, 16, 24, 37. Children answer with fingers, hands or a whispered number. Nobody writes. Joining cold: all you need is counting to 20.
@rec
Two sneak-peek puzzles: ideas we have not learnt yet. A guess is a great start, and I do not know is welcome. Nobody is marked.
Puzzle one. Count the stars. Write how many. You may draw rings round groups to help.
Children count the stars and write the number on their own paper.
Puzzle two. Mei has 3 bundles of ten sticks and 4 single sticks. Ben has 34 sticks. Could they have the same number? Write yes or no, and why.
Children write or draw their answer.
Everyone holds their paper to the camera at the same moment, once, after puzzle two. Do not read answers aloud. No private chat.
Thank you. We will come back to puzzle two in a few minutes.

Puzzle 1 answer: 24 stars. Puzzle 2 answer: yes, 3 tens and 4 ones is 34. Look for good ideas to praise later (a child who drew rings of ten, or who said 3 bundles is 30). Do not write scores or keep a list.
@rec
Today your hands are the teachers. Grab a handful of your small things, not the whole pile. Make bundles of ten. Count the bundles, then count the singles left over.
If you finish, try the what-if card: what if you open a bundle?
Round 1: each child grabs, bundles and counts. Tutor scans the cameras and asks a few children to show their bundles.
Tell me what you have. Say it like this: I have, how many tens, and how many ones.
Round two: show me! Use your tens bars and ones squares from the kit page. I call a number. You build it, then hold it up to the camera.
Seventeen.
Children build 17. Hold up to the camera on a count of three.
Thirty.
Build 30.
Forty-two.
Build 42.
Fifty-eight.
Build 58.
One more. Ravi built thirty-five with 5 bars and 3 squares. Look at your kit. Is Ravi right?
Children check with their kit and answer by thumbs up or down, then say why. Answer: no, 5 bars and 3 squares is 53; thirty-five is 3 bars and 5 squares.
What did you notice? How many singles can be left over? Could you have ten singles left over? Why not?
If you have ten singles you can tie them into another bundle. So the singles left over are always nought to nine.
A child who counts bundles as ones (3 bundles and 4 singles is 7): hold up a real bundle and say, this one is worth ten. Count it: ten, twenty, thirty, then thirty-one, thirty-two.
A child with too few things: use the kit bars and squares for round 1 as well.

Main room only: no breakout rooms in this lesson, so you can see every camera. Pairs are optional: a grown-up may check the building. Building with the kit is for every child; the what-if card is for any child who wants it, and nobody is named.
@rec
Look. Ten single sticks. When I tie them together I have one bundle. One bundle is worth ten.
How many sticks are in one bundle?
Here are 3 bundles and 4 singles. I count the bundles in tens: ten, twenty, thirty. Then I count the singles: thirty-one, thirty-two, thirty-three, thirty-four. Thirty-four sticks.
I write it in two boxes. Tens: 3. Ones: 4. That makes 34. The left digit counts the tens. The right digit counts the ones.
Which digit tells me how many bundles?
Your turn. Write the number for each picture on your paper.
Children write three numbers.
Twenty-seven, forty, nineteen.
Look at forty. 4 bundles and no singles. We write a zero in the ones box. If we left it out, the 4 would look like 4 ones. The zero holds the place.
Two six and six two use the same digits. Which has more sticks, 26 or 62? How do you know?
The tens digit is worth more. 62 has 6 bundles. 26 has only 2 bundles. The order of the digits matters.
Sometimes you have lots of singles. Here are 2 bundles and 13 singles. Ten of the singles can tie into a new bundle. Now there are 3 bundles and 3 singles. Same sticks, 33 of them.
Why can we tie up ten singles? What is a bundle worth?
Quick-fire. I say a number. You tell me the tens and the ones. Forty-seven.
Sixty?
Nineteen?
Eighty-two?
Count together: tens, then ones: 10, 20, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34.

Key words to use every time: bundle (ten), single (one), tens digit, ones digit. Do not teach 'place value' as a term yet. Do not teach carrying. Keep ten singles making a bundle for the Think harder page.
If a child reads 34 as 43: ask them to build it with the kit bars and squares and say the tens first.
@rec
Stand up and get a sip of water. A big jump for every ten, a small hop for every one. Thirty-four is three big jumps and four small hops.
Call 12, 25, 40, 31. Children jump the tens and hop the ones. Count the jumps and hops aloud together.
@rec
Page 1, Start here. Question 1: count the sticks and fill in the bundles, the singles and the number. Question 2: draw 3 bundles and 5 singles. Question 3: write the numbers.
Page 1, questions 1 to 3. Tutor walks the cameras, asks how do you know. Wait 10 seconds before helping.
Twenty-six. Thirty-five. Forty-two, seventy, nineteen, eighty-five. Mark your own page in another colour.
After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder. Everyone may choose, at any time.
Page 2. Question 4: fill in tens and ones. Question 5: Ali has 47 straws. Question 6: Siti wrote 43. Is she right? Question 7: draw Ali's 6 bundles and Mei's 6 singles, and write each number.
Page 2, questions 4 to 7.
Five tens and eight ones. Four tens, no ones. Seven tens and one one. Four bundles, seven left over. Siti should write thirty-four. Question 7: Ali has sixty, Mei has six.
When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation. Everyone may choose. You can swap at any time.
Choice time: Think harder (page 3), Go further (page 4), the Investigation (page 5), or finish and check your own work. Tutor never says who is on which page.

Q2 (drawing): draw a bundle as ten short lines with a ring round them. Q4 (zero): ask how many singles are left over in 40. Q6: build 3 bundles and 4 singles with the kit, say the tens first. Q7: ask how much one bundle is worth.

A child who is still stuck ticks 'I am still stuck' on the look-back page. You check in during the open session in the next lesson (a quick visit to the shared room or a hand signal, parent nearby). Never a private message.
Think harder is for ideas taught today in a new setting. Go further is for mastery and extension. Do not announce who is on which page. Pairs are never split unless both children agree.
@rec
Mei says 26 and 62 are the same, because they use the same digits. Do you agree? Use bundles to explain.
Build 26 and 62 with your kit bars and squares. Which one has more?
Talk to the grown-up next to you or to your screen for one minute. Use the sentence starter: I think... because...
Who would like to share? Volunteers first. A pass is always fine.
Remember puzzle two? Mei has 3 bundles and 4 singles. Ben has 34 sticks. Yes! They have the same number, thirty-four.
Did anyone change their mind about puzzle two while we worked? You can just nod.

Model answer: No. 26 is 2 bundles and 6 singles. 62 is 6 bundles and 2 singles. 62 has more sticks. Volunteers first; never call a child by name to answer; no tallies, no rankings. Praise the reason, not the speed.
@rec
Exit ticket. Three questions, on your own, without looking back. Write your answers on page 5.
Children answer E1 to E3 on their own.
Everyone holds their ticket to the camera at the same moment so only you see it. No private chat.
Forty-eight. Three tens and seven ones. Seventy, and the zero is needed to show there are no ones.
Check your own ticket in a different colour. Well done. I will stamp your inquiry journal.

Mark S, D or H in the tutor tracker (tutor only): S = secure on all three, D = developing (one wrong), H = needs help (two or three wrong). If D or H, plan two minutes of catch-up at the start of Lesson 2, in the open session, no names. Do not read out any child's result.
@rec
Look-back. Tick what was hard and what helped you. Write or draw one thing you did well. If you like, tick one thing to try next time. You can pass. Nobody reads it out.
Children fill in the look-back box on page 5.
Well done, inquirers. Next lesson is Number Words and the Number Line. You need only a pencil and paper. Goodbye, and thank you to the grown-ups.
Optional, only if you are on time: what is the biggest number you can make with 9 bundles and 9 singles? And what happens if you add one more single?
Short think time, then take two answers.
Spare-time menu. If the whole class is ahead, pick one or two activities from the guide (about 4 minutes each).

This is the standing buffer. If you are behind, finish the look-back and say goodbye. Do not start anything new. Optional slide answer: 99; one more is ten bundles, which is called a hundred (next lessons). If the whole class is ahead, use the Spare-time menu (guide section 3) instead of rushing on.

slides.title: Bundles and Singles
slides.subtitle: Whole numbers: tens and ones

blocks.head: TODAY WE WILL
items: Make bundles of ten, and use them to read and write numbers.

slides.note: Lesson 1 of Term 1, 90 minutes. Objective: read and write two-digit numbers as bundles of ten and single ones. Time plan: opening 0 to 4, warm-up 4 to 10, sneak-peek 10 to 14, explore 14 to 28, mini-lesson 28 to 38, brain break 38 to 42, workbook 42 to 70, talk 70 to 76, exit ticket 76 to 82, look-back 82 to 85, flex time and goodbye 85 to 90 (the buffer: do not start anything new). Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are for every child to choose. Nobody is told which page they should be on. Tell the group the lesson is recorded (you and the screen only) and that a child may keep the camera off.

mascot.say: Hi, I'm Mi. Let's notice, test and explain why!

slides.title: Our lesson today

rows: Count in tens and show ten with fingers
Two puzzles. A guess is fine.

slides.note: Show this for about 20 seconds and name the phases only; do not read the table. Lesson 1 only: it introduces the routine every lesson follows.

slides.title: Four inquirer rules

items: Notice it. Look closely.
Test it. Try it with real things.
Explain why. Say how you know.
Mistakes help us. A guess is fine. You can pass.

blocks.head: RECORDING
items: We record the tutor and the screen only. You may keep your camera off.

slides.note: Read the four rules together. Say the recording notice in your own words: the platform records the tutor and the shared screen; children's video is excluded; names are kept off the screen. A parent or child who does not wish to be in the recording can keep the camera off. Then tell the shopkeeper story (47 pencils) and ask the group what a shopkeeper could do.

slides.title: Warm-up: count in tens

blocks.text: Clap on every number
Now count back from 100. Whisper, and shout on 50!

slides.note: Count in tens to 100 with a clap on each number, then back to 0. This is a spiral review of skip counting in tens (holiday topic) and lets a new child join: they hear it before they say it.

slides.title: Fingers to ten

blocks.text: I show 6. How many more fingers make 10?

slides.note: Say each number; children show on their fingers how many more make ten. Answers: 6 needs 4, 3 needs 7, 8 needs 2, 5 needs 5, 9 needs 1. Hands up on camera is fine. No writing, no marks.

slides.title: Ten and some more

blocks.text: 10 and 3 more is ___

slides.note: Answers: 13, 16, 24, 37. Say the tens word slowly, then the ones: twenty... four. This is the bridge to bundles of ten and singles. Show 20 and 30 as two or three full ten-frames if a child is unsure.

slides.title: Sneak-peek puzzles

blocks.text: Ideas we have not learnt yet. A guess is a great start. Nobody is marked.

cols.head: PUZZLE 1: anyone can try
items: Count the stars. Write how many.
You may draw rings round groups.

cols.head: PUZZLE 2: think
items: Mei has 3 bundles of ten sticks and 4 single sticks.
Ben has 34 sticks.
Could they have the same number? Write yes or no, and why.

slides.note: Puzzle 1 (24 stars) is an access question: any child can try it by counting or drawing rings. Puzzle 2 is a thinking question on the lesson's key idea. Say: two sneak-peek puzzles, ideas we have not learnt yet; a guess is a great start and I do not know is welcome; nobody is marked. Children write on their own paper. Everyone holds the paper to the camera once, at the same moment, after puzzle 2; there is no private chat and no board in front of the group. Answers: 24; yes (3 tens and 4 ones is 34). Do not reveal Puzzle 2 until Talk time. Do not write scores or keep a list of who found it easy.

slides.title: Explore: grab and bundle

items: Grab a handful of small things. Not the whole pile.
Make bundles of ten: a band, a cup, or a ring on paper.
Count the bundles. Count the singles left over.
Say: I have ___ tens and ___ ones.

blocks.head: WHAT IF?
items: What if you open a bundle? Can you show your number a different way?

slides.note: Round 1, about 4 minutes. Objects first, no writing yet. Children bundle in tens and count the singles. Ask a few children to show their bundles to the camera. The what-if card is available from the start so nobody waits: it previews the Think harder idea (opening a bundle), and no child is named for choosing it. A child with too few things can use the kit bars and squares.

slides.title: Show me!

blocks.text: Build each number with your tens bars and ones squares. Hold it up to the camera when I count to three.

blocks.label: a bar is a ten, a square is a one

slides.note: Round 2, about 4 minutes, main room. Call each number aloud and show it on the slide. Children build with the kit bars (tens) and squares (ones). On a count of three, everyone holds their build to the camera. Check the zero case (30) and the larger ones (42, 58). Answers: 17 is 1 bar and 7 squares; 30 is 3 bars; 42 is 4 bars and 2 squares; 58 is 5 bars and 8 squares.

slides.title: What did we notice?

items: How many singles can be left over?
Could you have ten singles left over? Why not?
Is it quicker to count 40 singles, or 4 tens?

slides.note: Take one or two answers from volunteers. Key idea: the singles left over are always 0 to 9, because ten singles tie into another bundle. Counting in tens is quicker and easier to keep track of. Repeat a child's answer in your own words so the recording picks it up.

slides.title: Ten singles make a bundle

blocks.text: 10 singles = 1 bundle of ten

slides.note: Show ten single sticks, then tie them into one bundle. A bundle is worth ten. Ask: how many sticks are in one bundle? Answer: ten.

slides.title: Reading 34

blocks.text: 30 and 4 more is 34. The left digit counts the tens. The right digit counts the ones.

slides.note: Think aloud: count the bundles in tens (10, 20, 30) then the singles (31, 32, 33, 34). Write 3 in the tens box and 4 in the ones box. Ask: which digit tells me how many bundles? Answer: the left one, 3.

slides.title: Your turn: write the number

blocks.text: Write on your paper. Timer: 1 minute

slides.note: Each child writes on their own paper. Walk the cameras. Do not ask children to hold boards up in front of the group.

slides.title: Check: write the number
slides.note: Answers: 27, 40, 19. Read each answer aloud so a child watching the recording can mark their own work.

slides.title: The zero holds the place

blocks.text: No singles, so the ones box has a 0. Without the 0, 4 would look like 4 ones.

slides.note: Zero ones means no singles. The zero is needed so the 4 stays in the tens place. A common slip is to write 4 for 4 tens.

slides.title: Same digits, different number

blocks.text: Which has more sticks? How do you know?

slides.note: 26 is 2 bundles and 6 singles. 62 is 6 bundles and 2 singles. 62 has more because the tens digit is worth more. The order of the digits matters. This sets up the Talk time question.

slides.title: Ten singles can tie up

blocks.text: 13 ones = 1 ten and 3 ones

slides.note: Show 2 bundles and 13 singles, then tie ten of the singles into a third bundle: 3 bundles and 3 singles. Both pictures are 33 sticks. This is the idea Think harder uses (5 tens and 14 ones). Keep it to about a minute: it is a worked example, not a new skill to drill.

slides.title: Count: tens, then ones

blocks.text: Say it together

slides.note: Count the 3 bundles then the 4 singles together. This is the same count as the explore. Keep it short.

slides.title: Jump the tens, hop the ones

blocks.text: A big jump for every ten. A small hop for every one.
34 is 3 big jumps and 4 small hops. Sip some water.

slides.note: Four minutes. Stand up on camera. Call each number and have children jump the tens and hop the ones; count the jumps and hops aloud. No equipment. Keep it gentle for small spaces.

slides.title: Workbook page 1: Start here

blocks.text: Questions 1 to 3. Timer: 8 minutes

slides.note: Read questions 1 and 2 aloud. Children work on their own; the tutor walks the cameras and asks how do you know. Wait 10 seconds before helping. After question 3 any child may choose to carry on or try Think harder.

slides.title: Check page 1
slides.note: Read each answer aloud. Children mark their own page in a different colour. Never ask a child to show a wrong answer to the group.

slides.title: Workbook page 2: Start here

blocks.text: Questions 4 to 7. Timer: 9 minutes

slides.note: Read question 6 aloud: it is a spot-the-mistake. Read question 7 aloud as well: draw Ali's and Mei's sticks. Children may draw bundles to decide.

slides.title: Check page 2
slides.note: Read each answer aloud so a child watching the recording can mark their own work. Question 6 answer: no, Siti should write 34, because 43 is 4 tens and 3 ones. Never ask a child to show a wrong answer to the group. Question 7 answer: Ali has 60 and Mei has 6, because 6 tens is much more than 6 ones.

slides.title: Choose your next page

rows: Our idea in a new setting
Finish and check your own work

blocks.text: Everyone may choose. You can swap at any time.

slides.note: Invite the whole group at once, for example: when you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation. Never announce who is on which page and never name a child. Pairs are not split unless both children agree. Model answers are in the tutor guide. About 4 minutes.

slides.title: Talk and explain

blocks.head: MEI SAYS
items: 26 and 62 are the same, because they use the same digits.

blocks.text: Do you agree? Use bundles to explain.
I think ... because ...

slides.note: One minute of talk to the grown-up next to you, or to your screen. Then volunteers first; a pass is always fine; never call a child by name to answer. Model answer: no. 26 is 2 bundles and 6 singles. 62 is 6 bundles and 2 singles, so 62 has more. Repeat each child's answer in your own words for the recording.

slides.title: Back to the sneak-peek

blocks.text: Yes! Mei and Ben can have the same number: 34.

slides.note: Reveal puzzle 2 now. Say: many of you wrote a good reason. Do not read out anyone's earlier answer.

slides.title: Exit ticket

blocks.text: On your own. No looking back. Timer: 3 minutes

slides.note: Children answer on page 5. After the timer everyone holds the ticket to the camera at the same moment, so only the tutor sees it (no private chat). Stamp the inquiry journal.

slides.title: Check the exit ticket
slides.note: Read each answer aloud. Children check their own ticket in a different colour.

slides.title: Look-back
slides.note: Three minutes. Children tick or write the look-back box on page 5. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out. If a child ticks I am still stuck, check in during the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared room or a hand signal, parent nearby); never a direct message. The Next time I will try row is optional; at the start of the next lesson you may say to the whole group: today you could try drawing it, using objects or checking your answer.

mascot.say: Take your time. You can pass.

slides.title: Well done, inquirers!

blocks.text: Show a grown-up one thing you found out today.

blocks.head: NEXT LESSON
items: Number Words and the Number Line
You need a pencil and paper.

slides.note: Say goodbye and thank the grown-ups. Minutes 85 to 90 are flex time: the buffer. If you ran late, finish any open item (stamps, the look-back). Do not start anything new. If the whole class is ahead, show the optional menu slide and use the Spare-time menu from the tutor guide.

slides.title: Go further: what if?

blocks.text: What is the biggest number you can make with 9 bundles and 9 singles?
What happens if you add one more single?

slides.note: Optional, only if you are on time. Answer: 99. One more single makes 10 singles, which tie into a tenth bundle: ten bundles. Ten tens have a name: a hundred (Lesson 2 onwards). Take two answers and move on.

slides.title: If we have time: pick one

rows: Add one more single. Does the ones digit always go up by one?
Write a mystery number puzzle for your grown-up
Show how to read 52 with bundles and singles

blocks.text: Optional. Everyone may join.

slides.note: Optional Spare-time menu, used only if the whole class is ahead. Pick one or two activities (3 to 5 minutes each); full tutor lines and answers are in the tutor guide. Never start new content and never name who is ahead. Slow down with how do you know rather than rushing on. These minutes come from the flex buffer and are not part of the 90-minute sum.

start.hint: Count the bundles in tens: 10, 20. Then count the singles on: 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26.
start.solution: Count the 2 bundles in tens: 10, 20. Then count on the 6 singles: 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26. So 2 bundles, 6 singles, 26 sticks.
mistakes: Writing the digits the wrong way round (62).

start.text: Draw 3 bundles of ten and 5 single sticks in the box. Then write the number.
start.answer: 35 (3 bundles drawn, each with ten sticks, and 5 singles)
start.hint: Draw a bundle as ten short lines with a ring round them. Draw 3 of those, then 5 more short lines on their own.
start.solution: Draw 3 rings each holding ten short lines (that is 30), then 5 single lines. Count: 10, 20, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35.
mistakes: Drawing 3 sticks and 5 sticks instead of 3 bundles of ten.

start.hint: Say the tens first, then the ones. In (d) the ones come first in the words, but the tens digit still goes on the left.
start.solution: (a) 4 tens is 40, and 2 more is 42. (b) 7 tens is 70 and there are no ones: 70. (c) 10 and 9 is 19. (d) 8 tens is 80, and 5 ones makes 85.

start.text: Fill in the tens and ones.
start.answer: 5 tens 8 ones; 4 tens 0 ones; 7 tens 1 one
start.hint: The left digit counts the tens. The right digit counts the ones. You can build it with your kit.
start.solution: (a) 58: the 5 is the tens digit, the 8 is the ones digit. (b) 40: 4 tens and no ones. (c) 71: 7 tens and 1 one.

start.text: Ali has 47 straws. He ties them into bundles of ten.

parts.text: How many full bundles can he make? ___
How many straws are left over? ___

start.hint: 47 is 4 tens and 7 ones. Draw it if you like.
start.solution: 47 is 4 tens and 7 ones, so Ali makes 4 full bundles and has 7 straws left over (4 bundles hold 40 straws).
mistakes: Saying 3 bundles and 17 left over: 17 singles can still make another bundle.

start.text: Siti has 3 bundles of ten and 4 single sticks. She writes 43. Is Siti right? Write the number she should write, and say what she mixed up.
start.answer: No. 34. She wrote the tens and ones digits the wrong way round (43 is 4 tens and 3 ones).
start.hint: Build 3 bundles and 4 singles with your kit. Say the tens first.
start.solution: 3 bundles is 30 and 4 singles makes 34. Siti wrote 43, which is 4 tens and 3 ones. The tens digit goes on the left.
mistakes: Saying she is right because the digits 3 and 4 are there.
Not saying what she mixed up (any clear sentence about the digits is fine).

start.text: Ali has 6 bundles of ten and no single sticks. Mei has 6 single sticks and no bundles. Draw what each child has in the box. Then write each number.
start.answer: Ali 60, Mei 6. Ali has more (6 tens is 60; 6 singles is 6)
start.hint: A bundle is worth ten. Count Ali's bundles in tens. Mei has no bundles, only ones.
start.solution: Ali: 6 bundles of ten is 60, with no singles, so 60. Mei: 6 single sticks is 6. The same digit 6 means very different amounts because of its place: 6 tens or 6 ones.
mistakes: Drawing 6 sticks for Ali instead of 6 bundles of ten.

think.text: Mei has 5 bundles of ten and 14 loose sticks. How many sticks has she? Hint: can she make another bundle?
think.answer: 64 (14 loose sticks make 1 more bundle and 4 left, so 6 tens and 4 ones)
think.hint: Take 10 of the loose sticks and tie them into a bundle. How many bundles now? How many singles?
think.solution: 14 loose sticks = 1 bundle and 4 singles. So Mei has 5 + 1 = 6 bundles and 4 singles: 64 sticks. Check: 50 + 14 = 64.

think.text: 41 is 4 tens and 1 one. Open one bundle. Now 41 is 3 tens and ___ ones.
think.hint: A bundle has ten sticks. If you open one, those ten sticks become singles, and you still have the 1 you had.
think.solution: Opening a bundle gives 10 more singles. 1 single + 10 singles = 11 singles, and 3 bundles are left. 30 + 11 = 41, so it is the same number.

think.text: Mystery number. Clue 1: I am between 30 and 50. Clue 2: my ones digit is 6. Clue 3: my number of tens is even. What number am I?
think.hint: List the numbers between 30 and 50 that end in 6. Then check the tens.
think.solution: Between 30 and 50 and ending in 6: 36 and 46. 36 has 3 tens (odd). 46 has 4 tens (even). So the number is 46.
mistakes: Stopping at 36 and not checking clue 3.

think.text: Mei has 7 tens and 2 ones. Ali has 6 tens and 12 ones. Who has more, or do they have the same? Show how you know.
think.answer: The same: 72 each (6 tens 12 ones is 7 tens 2 ones)
think.hint: Take 10 of Ali's 12 loose ones and tie them into a bundle. How many bundles and ones does Ali have now?
think.solution: Ali's 12 ones make 1 more bundle and 2 ones. So Ali has 7 tens and 2 ones, the same as Mei. Both have 72.
mistakes: Saying Ali has more because 12 is bigger than 2.

go.text: Ben has 6 bundles of ten and 14 loose sticks. Siti has 85 loose sticks. Who has more sticks? How many more?
go.answer: Siti. Ben has 74, Siti has 85, so Siti has 11 more.
go.hint: Work out Ben's number first. Remember 14 loose sticks make a bundle and 4 more.
go.solution: Ben: 6 tens and 14 ones is 7 tens and 4 ones, so 74. Siti: 85. 85 is 8 tens 5 ones and 74 is 7 tens 4 ones: 1 ten and 1 one more, which is 11 more.
mistakes: Comparing only 6 and 85 without working out Ben's whole number.
Not opening 14 ones into a bundle before comparing.

go.text: A shop sells pencils in boxes of ten. Mei needs 60 pencils. She has 4 full boxes and 18 loose pencils. How many more pencils does she need?
go.answer: 2 more pencils (4 boxes and 18 pencils is 58)
go.hint: First find how many pencils she has now. Remember that 18 loose pencils make 1 more box and 8 pencils.
go.solution: 4 boxes is 40 pencils. 40 + 18 = 58. She needs 60, so she needs 60 - 58 = 2 more.
mistakes: Forgetting the 4 full boxes hold 40 pencils.

go.text: How many different ways can you show 30 with bundles of ten and loose sticks, if you may open bundles? Write each way as ___ tens and ___ ones. (3 tens and 0 ones is one way.)
go.answer: 4 ways: 3 tens 0 ones; 2 tens 10 ones; 1 ten 20 ones; 0 tens 30 ones
go.hint: Start with 3 tens. Open one bundle. What do you have now? Keep going until there are no bundles.
go.solution: 3 tens 0 ones. Open one bundle: 2 tens 10 ones. Open another: 1 ten 20 ones. Open the last: 0 tens 30 ones. That is 4 ways. Each time one ten becomes 10 ones.
mistakes: Stopping at 3 tens 0 ones and 0 tens 30 ones (2 ways).

investigation.title: Swap the digits
investigation.first: Write 14 and 41. Which number has more sticks? Then try 26 and 62, 52 and 25, and 77.
investigation.text: Pick a two-digit number. Swap its two digits. Is the new number bigger, smaller or the same? Is it always one of these three? When does each happen?
investigation.answer: Three things can happen. If the tens digit is smaller than the ones digit (14, 26), swapping makes a bigger number (41, 62). If the tens digit is bigger (52, 91), swapping makes a smaller number (25, 19). If the two digits are the same (77), the number stays the same.
investigation.look_for: A child who tests several numbers, says what they notice and gives a reason using tens and ones. A number that ends in 0 (30) becomes 03, which is just 3, so it is smaller: this fits 'tens digit bigger'.
mistakes: Saying swapping always makes the number bigger (testing only 14 and 26).
Not testing a number with equal digits.

talk.question: Mei says 26 and 62 are the same, because they use the same digits. Do you agree? Use bundles to explain.
talk.answer: No. 26 is 2 bundles of ten and 6 singles. 62 is 6 bundles of ten and 2 singles. 62 has more sticks, because the tens digit counts bundles of ten.
talk.look_for: A reason that uses tens and ones (not just 'because 6 is bigger').

exit.text: Fill in the tens and ones.
exit.solution: The left digit 3 counts the tens, the right digit 7 counts the ones.

exit.text: Write the number: 7 tens and 0 ones. Why do we need the 0?
exit.answer: 70. The 0 shows there are no ones, and it keeps the 7 in the tens place (without it, it would look like 7 ones).
exit.solution: 7 bundles of ten and no singles is 70. The zero holds the ones place.

hardest: knowing which digit is the tens

home_practice.text: A box has 3 bundles of ten pencils and 8 loose pencils. How many pencils are there?

home_practice.solution: The left digit is the tens, the right digit is the ones.

home_practice.text: Write the number: 9 ones and 2 tens.
home_practice.solution: 2 tens is 20, and 9 ones makes 29. The tens digit goes first.

home_practice.text: Ben has 4 tens and 12 ones. Is that 52 or 412? Show how you know.
home_practice.answer: 52 (12 ones make 1 ten and 2 ones, so 5 tens and 2 ones)
home_practice.solution: Tie 10 of the 12 ones into a bundle: 5 bundles and 2 ones, which is 52.

home_practice.text: At home: find 30 to 50 small things (pasta, clips, buttons). Make bundles of ten with bands, cups or rings on paper. Write: ___ tens and ___ ones = ___ . Then open one bundle and write the number a different way.
home_practice.answer: Any: for example 3 tens and 7 ones = 37, and also 2 tens and 17 ones = 37. Check: tens x 10 + ones = how many things.
home_practice.solution: A grown-up counts the things one by one to check the number. Opening a bundle gives one fewer ten and ten more ones.

items.q: There are 3 bundles of ten sticks and 4 single sticks. How many sticks are there altogether?
items.hint: Count the bundles in tens (10, 20, 30), then count on the singles.

slips.say: 7 is 3 + 4. A bundle is worth ten, not one. Count the bundles in tens first.
43 is 4 tens and 3 ones. You have 3 bundles and 4 singles, so the 3 goes first.

tpl.q: There are {t} bundles of ten sticks and {o} single sticks. How many sticks are there altogether?
tpl.hint: Count the bundles in tens, then count on the {o} singles.

items.q: How many full bundles of ten can you make from 47 sticks?
items.hint: 47 is made of tens and ones. The left digit counts the tens.
steps: Each ten is one full bundle.
So you can make 4 full bundles.

slips.say: 7 is the number of singles left over. The question asks for the full bundles of ten.
47 is all the sticks. How many tens are in 47?

tpl.q: How many full bundles of ten can you make from {n} sticks?
tpl.hint: The left digit of {n} counts the tens.
steps: {n} is made of tens and ones.
The left digit counts the full bundles.
So you can make {ans} full bundles.

items.q: You tie 47 sticks into bundles of ten. How many single sticks are left over?
items.hint: The right digit counts the ones, the sticks that are not in a bundle.
steps: The 7 ones are left over as singles.

slips.say: 4 is the number of bundles. The question asks for the singles left over.

tpl.q: You tie {n} sticks into bundles of ten. How many single sticks are left over?
tpl.hint: The right digit of {n} counts the ones.
steps: {n} is made of tens and ones.
The tens are tied in bundles.

items.q: Write the number: 9 ones and 2 tens.
items.hint: The tens digit goes on the left, even though the question says the ones first.

slips.say: 92 is 9 tens and 2 ones. The question says 9 ones and 2 tens, so the 2 goes on the left.

tpl.q: Write the number: {o} ones and {t} tens.
tpl.hint: The tens digit goes on the left, even though the question says the ones first.

items.q: Write the number: 7 tens and 0 ones.
items.hint: No ones means the ones digit is 0. The 0 keeps the 7 in the tens place.
steps: There are no ones to add.

slips.say: 7 would be 7 ones. 7 tens needs a 0 in the ones place.
700 is far too big. 7 tens is 70.

tpl.q: Write the number: {t} tens and 0 ones.
tpl.hint: No ones means the ones digit is 0.
steps: There are no ones to add.

items.q: Which number is 4 tens and 6 ones?
items.hint: The tens digit goes on the left and the ones digit on the right.
steps: The left digit 4 counts the tens, the right digit 6 counts the ones.

slips.say: 64 is 6 tens and 4 ones. We need 4 tens first.

items.q: Mei has 5 bundles of ten and 14 loose sticks. How many sticks has she?
items.hint: Tie 10 of the loose sticks into another bundle. How many bundles and singles now?
steps: 14 loose sticks make 1 more bundle and 4 singles.
Now Mei has 5 + 1 = 6 bundles and 4 singles.

slips.say: 19 is 5 + 14. Bundles are worth ten each, so think of 5 tens first.
Do not join the numbers side by side. 5 bundles is 50, then add the 14.

tpl.q: Mei has {t} bundles of ten and {o} loose sticks. How many sticks has she?
tpl.hint: Tie 10 of the loose sticks into another bundle.
steps: {o} loose sticks make 1 more bundle and {r} singles.
Now Mei has {u} bundles and {r} singles.

items.q: 41 is 4 tens and 1 one. Open one bundle. Now 41 is 3 tens and how many ones?
items.hint: Opening a bundle gives you 10 more singles. You still have the 1 you started with.
steps: Open one bundle: 3 bundles are left.
The opened bundle gives 10 singles, plus the 1 single you had.
10 + 1 = 11 ones, so 41 is 3 tens and 11 ones.

slips.say: 10 is the opened bundle. Do not forget the 1 single you already had.
1 is the single you started with. The opened bundle gives 10 more.

tpl.q: {n} is {t} tens and {o} ones. Open one bundle. Now {n} is {u} tens and how many ones?
tpl.hint: Opening a bundle gives you 10 more singles. You still have the {o} you started with.
steps: Open one bundle: {u} bundles are left.
The opened bundle gives 10 singles, plus the {o} you had.

items.q: Mystery number. I am between 30 and 50. My ones digit is 6. My number of tens is even. What number am I?
items.hint: List the numbers between 30 and 50 that end in 6. Then check the tens.
steps: Between 30 and 50 and ending in 6: 36 and 46.

slips.say: 36 has 3 tens, and 3 is odd. Check clue 3.

items.q: Mei has 7 tens and 2 ones. Ali has 6 tens and 12 ones. Who has more?
items.hint: Tie 10 of Ali's 12 ones into a bundle. What does Ali have now?
steps: Ali's 12 ones make 1 bundle and 2 ones.
So Ali has 7 tens and 2 ones.
That is the same as Mei: 72.

slips.say: 12 is a big number of ones, but ten of them make a bundle. Tie them up and compare again.

items.q: Ben has 6 bundles of ten and 14 loose sticks. Siti has 85 loose sticks. How many more sticks does Siti have than Ben?
items.hint: Find Ben's number first. Then compare tens and ones.
steps: Ben: 6 tens and 14 ones is 7 tens and 4 ones, which is 74.
85 is 1 ten and 1 one more than 74, so Siti has 11 more.

slips.say: 14 is Ben's loose sticks. Work out Ben's whole number (74) first.
25 is 85 - 60. Ben also has 14 loose sticks.

tpl.q: Ben has {t} bundles of ten and {o} loose sticks. Siti has {s} loose sticks. How many more sticks does Siti have than Ben?
tpl.hint: Find Ben's whole number first, then compare it with {s}.
steps: Ben has {t} tens and {o} ones. Tie up ten of the ones to find his number.

items.q: A shop sells pencils in boxes of ten. Mei needs 60 pencils. She has 4 full boxes and 18 loose pencils. How many more pencils does she need?
items.hint: Work out how many pencils she has now. Then see how far it is from 60.

slips.say: 18 is the loose pencils she already has. Add the 4 boxes first (40).
42 is 60 - 18. She also has 4 full boxes.

tpl.q: A shop sells pencils in boxes of ten. Mei needs {N} pencils. She has {b} full boxes and {l} loose pencils. How many more pencils does she need?
tpl.hint: Work out how many pencils she has now, then see how far that is from {N}.

items.q: How many different ways can you show 30 with bundles of ten and loose sticks, if you may open bundles? (3 tens and 0 ones is one way.)
items.hint: Start with 3 tens and open one bundle at a time.
steps: Open one bundle: 2 tens and 10 ones. Open another: 1 ten and 20 ones. Open the last: 0 tens and 30 ones.

slips.say: There are more ways between 3 tens and 0 tens. Open the bundles one at a time.
Count 0 tens and 30 ones too.

tpl.q: How many different ways can you show {n} with bundles of ten and loose sticks, if you may open bundles?
tpl.hint: Start with all the tens. Open one bundle at a time until there are none left.
steps: Start with the full tens of {n}.
Open one bundle at a time until there are no bundles left.

items.q: Make up your own mystery number puzzle with 3 clues (between which two numbers, the ones digit, and odd or even tens). Check that only ONE number fits.
items.hint: Pick a secret number first. Then write clues that are true for it.
steps: Check your secret number fits every clue.
List the numbers that fit the first two clues. Cross out any that break clue 3.

Exactly one number should be left. For example: between 60 and 80, ones digit 3, an even number of tens. The numbers ending in 3 are 63 and 73. 63 has 6 tens (even) and 73 has 7 tens (odd), so only 63 fits.

parent.summary: We learned that a two-digit number is made of bundles of ten and single ones. Your child made bundles from real things, built numbers up to 58, and practised reading and writing numbers like 34 (3 tens and 4 ones) and 70 (7 tens and 0 ones).
words: bundle or ten: ten single things tied together
single or one: a thing on its own
tens digit: the left digit, it counts the bundles
ones digit: the right digit, it counts the singles
try_home: Bundle it: grab a handful of pasta, clips or buttons. Tie bundles of ten with bands or cups. Ask: how many tens and how many ones? Write the number together.
Show me: say a number up to 60 and let your child build it with bundles and singles. Swap roles and make a mistake on purpose for them to find.
Spot it: look at page numbers, lift buttons or door numbers. Ask: how many tens is that? Which digit tells you?
ask: Which digit tells how many bundles?
What if you opened a bundle?
parent.when_stuck: Please let your child use real things or draw bundles, and wait 10 seconds before helping. Asking 'what could you try?' works better than giving the answer.
parent.next: Lesson 2: Number Words and the Number Line. Your child needs a pencil and paper only.
parent.report_line: Your child is learning to see numbers as tens and ones and to say why. This week: reading and writing two-digit numbers from bundles of ten and single ones.
parent.term_line: Your child is learning to see numbers as tens and ones, to notice patterns and to say why.

safeguarding: Small things stay on the table: nothing goes in the mouth or ears. No matches, toothpicks or anything sharp. Use hair ties, cups or paper rings, not stretched rubber bands that can flick.
This lesson uses the main room only: no breakout rooms, so the tutor sees every camera. A parent sits nearby but does not give answers.
Sneak-peek and exit answers are shown on the child's own paper to the camera at the same moment, once. There is no private chat and no board held up in front of the group.
Never read out a child's name with a right or wrong answer. Never show a child's page in the recording; record the tutor and the screen only, with children's video excluded.
A child who ticks 'I am still stuck' gets a check-in in the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared room or a hand signal, parent nearby). No private messages to children.
The look-back is never collected in front of the group or read out. A pass is always allowed.
tutor_prep: Solve every workbook question yourself first.
Tell parents a week before: print workbook pages 1 to 6, cut out the kit page (page 6), find about 50 small things and 6 hair ties or cups.
Have the slides open and check the timer slide and the kit page are visible on screen share.
Check the recording settings exclude children's video.

spare_time.note: Optional time, never added to the 90-minute sum. It comes from the 5-minute flex buffer, from slack in the parts, or from the optional Go further slide.
rules: Whole class ahead: use the Spare-time menu in the Flex time and the optional Go further slide. Pick one or two activities; do not start new content.
A few children ahead: they may choose Go further or the Investigation, which are open to everyone. Never label or name a child, and never announce who is ahead.
Never teach anything the next lesson needs. If the class is ahead, slow down: ask 'How do you know?' and let children explain, rather than rushing on.

menu.title: Is it always true?
menu.tutor: Mei says: if you add one more single stick, the ones digit goes up by one. Is that always true? Try 23, 47 and 39 with your sticks or kit.
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Try 23, 47 and 39 with one more single each. Is Mei always right?
menu.answer: Not always. 23 and 47 become 24 and 48. 39 plus one single makes ten singles, which tie into a new bundle: 40. It is true unless the ones digit is 9.

menu.title: Make a puzzle for your grown-up
menu.tutor: Pick a secret number. Write two clues about its tens and its ones, like: it has 4 bundles and the ones digit is 7. Give it to your grown-up to solve.
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Write a mystery number puzzle with two clues for a grown-up to solve.
menu.answer: No single answer. Check that the clues fit the secret number and fit only one number.

menu.title: Teach it back
menu.tutor: Pretend your grown-up or a toy has never seen bundles. Teach them how to read 52 using bundles and singles.
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Teach a grown-up how to read 52 with bundles and singles.
menu.answer: 52 is 5 bundles of ten and 2 singles. The left digit counts the bundles, the right digit counts the singles.
